prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

cluster.label: Snowball Stemmer for multilingual stemming in NLTK
cluster.rationale: This candidate presents the Snowball Stemmer, its language support, and comparison with Porter Stemmer.

clusters.label: Snowball Stemmer for multilingual stemming in NLTK
clusters.rationale: This candidate presents the Snowball Stemmer, its language support, and comparison with Porter Stemmer.

clusters.label: Lemmatization with WordNetLemmatizer in NLTK
clusters.rationale: This candidate describes lemmatization using WordNet, contrasting with stemming and explaining prerequisites.

clusters.label: spaCy pipeline initialization and text processing
clusters.rationale: These candidates form the foundation of spaCy usage: creating a blank pipeline, processing text into a Doc, and understanding tokens and spans. They are closely related.

clusters.label: Lexical attributes and pattern detection in spaCy
clusters.rationale: This candidate uses token attributes like like_num to find patterns (e.g., percentages). It builds on basic token access but focuses on attribute-driven detection.

clusters.label: Loading pre-trained pipelines and their components in spaCy
clusters.rationale: These candidates cover loading trained pipelines (spacy.load) and understanding pipeline package contents (config, weights, strings.json). Both are about pre-trained models.

clusters.label: Predicting part-of-speech tags and dependencies in spaCy
clusters.rationale: This candidate focuses on extracting .pos_ and .dep_ from tokens after processing with a trained pipeline.

clusters.label: Named entity recognition and manual correction in spaCy
clusters.rationale: These candidates involve predicting named entities (doc.ents) and the capability to manually correct missed entities by creating Spans. Both address entity handling.

clusters.label: Rule-based matching with Matcher in spaCy
clusters.rationale: These candidates cover the Matcher for defining token-based patterns, from basic literal matches to complex linguistic patterns with lemmas and operators.

clusters.label: Introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP) concepts and challenges
clusters.rationale: This candidate provides a high-level overview of NLP, its statistical nature, and common applications. It sets the context but is distinct from tool-specific tasks.

clusters.label: spaCy overview: production-ready NLP library
clusters.rationale: This candidate describes spaCy's origin, license, focus on production, and multilingual support. It is an introductory overview.

clusters.label: spaCy model types: blank vs pre-trained and size trade-offs
clusters.rationale: This candidate explains the difference between blank and pre-trained models and the speed/accuracy trade-offs of model sizes.

clusters.label: Tokenization in spaCy: dividing text into linguistic units
clusters.rationale: This candidate defines tokenization, emphasizes language-specific tokenizers, and shows how to view tokens.

candidates.label: Snowball Stemmer for multilingual stemming
candidates.description: Snowball Stemmer is a stemming algorithm that supports multiple languages and often produces more accurate stems than Porter Stemmer, as shown by stemming 'generously' to 'generous' vs 'gener'.
coverage_criteria: Can list several languages supported by SnowballStemmer.
Can initialize SnowballStemmer with a language and stem a word.
Can explain why Snowball Stemmer might be preferred over Porter Stemmer.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates SnowballStemmer, its language support, and compares its output with Porter Stemmer on 'generously'.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Snowball Stemmer is a distinct tool with multilingual capability, a focused concept within stemming.

candidates.label: WordNet Lemmatizer for dictionary-based lemmatization
candidates.description: WordNetLemmatizer reduces words to their base dictionary form (lemma) using the WordNet lexical database. It requires NLTK data download (wordnet corpora). Unlike stemming, lemmas are actual words (e.g., 'flies' -> 'fly').
coverage_criteria: Can explain the difference between lemmatization and stemming.
Can instantiate WordNetLemmatizer and lemmatize a word.
Can identify that lemmatization depends on a lexical database like WordNet.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates lemmatization using WordNetLemmatizer, shows outputs on plural words, and contrasts with stemming implicitly.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Lemmatization is a key NLP normalization technique; this candidate captures its NLTK implementation and prerequisites, suitable for assessment.

candidates.label: Initializing a spaCy pipeline and processing text into a Doc
candidates.description: Use spacy.blank to create a language-specific pipeline and call it with a string to obtain a Doc object.
coverage_criteria: Write code to create a blank Portuguese pipeline 'nlp', process the string 'Olá mundo', and confirm the result is a Doc.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Sections 2 and 3 guide the student through creating blank pipelines for multiple languages and processing text, demonstrating the fundamental workflow.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single, atomic operation that is the prerequisite for all further spaCy processing.

candidates.label: Tokens and spans in spaCy
candidates.description: A Doc is a sequence of Token objects; a Span is a slice of the Doc. Access tokens by index.
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc for 'três cachorros e dois gatos', write code to retrieve the first token and create a span for 'três cachorros'.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 3 explicitly teaches the Doc, Token, and Span concepts through exercises.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Understanding the basic data structures is foundational and can be checked by asking for specific token and span retrieval.

candidates.label: Lexical attributes for pattern detection
candidates.description: Token attributes like `like_num` can identify numeric tokens. Combine attributes to find patterns like percentages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to find tokens that represent numbers in a Doc using `like_num`. Write a loop to detect a number followed by a '%' sign.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 4 uses `like_num` and `token.i+1` to find percentages, teaching how to use lexical attributes.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept is a specific, actionable technique for identifying patterns, not a broad overview.

candidates.label: Loading pre-trained NLP pipelines
candidates.description: Use `spacy.load` to load a trained pipeline (e.g., `pt_core_news_sm`) that can predict linguistic annotations.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load the Portuguese small pipeline and process a text, then print the Doc's text.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 7 demonstrates loading the Portuguese pipeline with `spacy.load`.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single step that enables access to pre-trained models, a key functionality of spaCy.

candidates.label: Components of a trained pipeline package
candidates.description: Trained pipelines include config.cfg (language and settings), binary weights for predictions, and strings.json (vocabulary mapping), but do not include the original training data.
coverage_criteria: List what is included in a spaCy pipeline package and explain why training data is not needed for predictions.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 6 explains that training data is NOT included and describes config, weights, and strings.json.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific factual knowledge point about pipeline packaging, suitable for a short comprehension check.

candidates.label: Predicting part-of-speech tags and dependencies
candidates.description: After processing text with a trained pipeline, each token has a .pos_ (coarse POS tag) and .dep_ (dependency label).
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc from a Portuguese pipeline, write a loop to print each token's text, .pos_, and .dep_.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 8, Part 1 has the student iterate tokens and print .pos_ and .dep_.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This focuses on two specific annotation types that are commonly used together.

candidates.label: Predicting named entities
candidates.description: Trained pipelines can identify named entities in a Doc. Access them via doc.ents and get their text and label (.label_).
coverage_criteria: Write code to iterate over doc.ents and print entity text and label. Use spacy.explain to describe a label.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 8, Part 2 and Section 9 demonstrate iterating entities and handling missed entities.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Named entity recognition is a distinct NLP task that can be practiced independently.

candidates.label: Manual correction of model predictions
candidates.description: When a trained model fails to recognize an entity, you can manually create a Span for the missed tokens.
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc where 'iPhone X' is not recognized, write code to create a Span for those two tokens.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 9 explicitly instructs the student to create a span for 'iPhone X' when the model misses it.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This teaches a practical workaround and emphasizes that models are not perfect, which is a valuable lesson.

candidates.label: Rule-based matching with Matcher
candidates.description: The Matcher class allows finding token sequences based on patterns defined with token attributes and operators.
coverage_criteria: Write code to initialize a Matcher, add a pattern that matches 'iPhone X', apply it to a Doc, and print the matched spans.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 11 walks through creating a Matcher, adding a pattern, and retrieving matches for 'iPhone X'.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a focused tool for rule-based matching, distinct from statistical predictions.

candidates.label: Writing complex match patterns
candidates.description: Patterns can use lemmas (LEMMA), POS tags, and quantifiers (e.g., '+', '*', '?') to match flexible sequences.
coverage_criteria: Write a pattern that matches a verb lemma 'baixar' followed by a proper noun, and a pattern for an adjective followed by one or two nouns.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Section 12 provides three exercises requiring patterns with lemmas, POS, and operators.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This advances from simple literal matching to linguistic-aware patterns, a key skill for information extraction.

candidates.label: Processamento de Linguagem Natural (PLN) – conceito e desafios
candidates.description: PLN é a área que estuda como fazer computadores entenderem línguas naturais. Por ser um problema não computável, as soluções são baseadas em aproximações estatísticas, resultando em incertezas e falsos positivos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar que PLN trata da compreensão de linguagem natural por máquinas.
Mencionar que as abordagens são estatísticas e aproximadas.
Dar exemplos de aplicações como extração de informações de documentos ou chatbots.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo dedica os primeiros minutos a definir PLN, contrastar com a leitura humana e destacar os desafios (aproximação estatística).
rationale.granularity_rationale: Conceito fundamental para contextualizar todo o restante do processamento de texto; um aluno precisa entender o propósito e limitações antes de usar ferramentas.

candidates.label: spaCy – biblioteca de PLN pronta para produção
candidates.description: spaCy é uma biblioteca open-source (MIT) para PLN, mantida pela Explosion.ai. Lançada em 2016, suporta 73 idiomas e é focada em uso em produção, com modelos pré-treinados de diferentes tamanhos.
coverage_criteria: Identificar o spaCy como biblioteca de PLN com foco em produção.
Diferenciar spaCy de outras bibliotecas como NLTK (acadêmico).
Citar que suporta múltiplos idiomas e oferece modelos pequenos, médios e grandes.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo apresenta o spaCy, sua origem, licença, mantenedores e diferenciais em relação a outras bibliotecas.
rationale.granularity_rationale: É necessário que o aluno saiba o que é o spaCy e suas características antes de usar a biblioteca.

anchors: Instalação e uso básico do spaCy

candidates.label: Modelos spaCy: blank vs pré-treinados e tamanhos
candidates.description: O spaCy permite criar modelos em branco (blank) com regras específicas de um idioma, ou carregar modelos pré-treinados (sm, md, lg) que já vêm com pesos estatísticos. Modelos maiores oferecem mais acurácia, mas são mais lentos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar a diferença entre blank('pt') e load('pt_core_news_lg').
Dizer que modelos pré-treinados incluem pesos para tarefas como POS e NER.
Comparar trade-offs de tamanho (pequeno, médio, grande) em velocidade e acurácia.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo mostra a diferença entre blank e pré-treinado, e discute os tamanhos (12MB, 40MB, 541MB) e a relação eficiência vs acurácia.
rationale.granularity_rationale: O conceito é básico para iniciar o uso do spaCy e escolher o modelo adequado para uma tarefa.

candidates.label: Tokenização – como o spaCy divide o texto em unidades
candidates.description: Tokenização é o processo de dividir um texto em unidades linguísticas chamadas tokens (palavras, pontuação, etc.). Cada língua tem seu próprio tokenizador. Tokens são a base para análises como POS e dependências.
coverage_criteria: Definir tokenização e dar exemplos de tokens (palavras, pontos).
Explicar que o tokenizador depende do idioma.
Usar list(doc) para visualizar os tokens de uma frase.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo destaca a tokenização como a primeira etapa essencial, mostrando como o spaCy separa 'Eduardo foi à feira.' em tokens e discute regras específicas do português.
rationale.granularity_rationale: É um conceito fundamental e isolável; pode ser verificado com uma simples pergunta sobre o resultado de tokenizar uma frase.

anchors: Tokenização: Base para entender o contexto

accepted_concepts.label: Specific teachable idea
accepted_concepts.description: What the student needs to understand.
coverage_criteria: Observable check in one to three focused questions.
accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: Why these candidates belong together or stand alone.

candidate_assignments.explanation: Why it should not stand alone but is represented by the accepted concept.
Why this candidate should not influence the graph.
Why this candidate should not influence the graph.

output_contract.review_policy: Do not use review except for structurally impossible inputs; Phase 4b repairs review outputs.

web_access_policy.instruction: Do not use web search or open URLs. Use only the provided candidate cards.
